newsitem.title: USA: Milken urges men to take control of prostate ills.
newsitem.headline: Milken urges men to take control of prostate ills.

text.p: In 1993 when he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, one-time junk bond king Michael Milken set out with a vengeance to solve the problem.
Three years later at age 49, he did so by aggressively taking control of his own medical care. Other men can do the same, Milken told Reuters in an interview.
Milken appeared at a weekend health care forum for prostate cancer sponsored by the American Cancer Society that attracted about 450 mostly middle-aged and elderly men.

Experts said such forums are becoming more important under managed care in which doctors spend less time and money discussing with their patients the rapidly increasing array of treatment options. At the same time the numbers of new prostate cancer patients is rising.

Milken, who served two years in prison and paid $1 billion in fines and settlements after pleading guilty in 1990 to securities-related crimes, has emerged as an advocate for patients facing prostate cancer. His federal probation is due to end Oct. 25.
At the Florida conference, he appeared tan and fit and was enthusiastically greeted by the audience after his speech.

Prostate cancer now fulfils most of the criteria of being an epidemic and will only get worse as the U.S. population ages, according to the American Cancer Society. Just as one in nine American women is expected to develop breast cancer in her lifetime, one in nine U.S. men is expected to develop prostate cancer, the organisation said.
In 1995, 244,000 new prostate cancer cases were diagnosed in the United States and last year another 317,000 were diagnosed. And like breast cancer, early detection means a higher cure rate.

However, Medicare does not cover the special blood test for prostate cancer nor do many managed care plans. And while doctors are legally mandated to inform a woman diagnosed with breast cancer of her treatment options, doctors are not obligated to do the same for men with prostate cancer, said Nina Entrekin, director of medical affairs for the American Cancer Society's Florida office.
Compounding the problem is that men often take a stoical approach and do not talk about this symptomless cancer.

"What you find is many men don't want to know," Milken said. "The concept is, if you don't know, it doesn't exist, and it's going to go away. My message is you can do something to change the course of your own disease."
Many of the men diagnosed with prostate cancer are over 65 and accustomed to leaving their health in the hands of doctors.

With the rapidly growing array of treatments available -- each one with a benefit to a particular patient depending on his age, severity of cancer and family situation -- a patient needs to research and decide what treatment is best for him.

"It's important that patients be aware a surgeon may be more likely to recommend surgery than a radiation therapist who might recommend radiation therapy. Part of this is not so much bias driven by their personal desires but by the uncertainty that exists," said Dr. David Bostwick, author of a new American Cancer Society book on prostate cancer to be released later this month, "Prostate Cancer What Every Man -- and His Family -- Needs to Know".
Unlike most patients, Milken took control of his treatment. "Do I believe stress played an important role? Yes," he said. "I dramatically changed my life."
He researched the treatment options available, first undergoing hormone therapy to shrink his cancer, then radiation therapy.

"I eliminated almost all fat in my diet and increased intake of soy and tofu, which appears to slow the growth of cancer," Milken said. Then, he began a regimen of daily massage and meditation, and other techniques to "fire up" his body's immune system.

Milken's same fervor that once created a financial powerhouse has now built the world's largest private cancer research foundation. His Santa Monica association, called CaP CURE, has given more than $20 million in grants to researchers during the past three years.
